meat products are more popular than more healthier foods. Another thing I noticed is that meat
products, like chicken, have gotten more popular over the years.

thing I wonder is how our diet affects the environment since our food costs a lot of water.

contributing to the statistics in these graphs.

I would use "Our diet's drastic change over time!".

raw_comment:
What I notice about both graphs is how rapidly meat is rising through both diet and the amount of water it needs to be made. In the first graph I noticed how both chicken and cheese increased throughout the 1980’s- 1990’s. It was also advised in the second graph that both the chicken and cheese are the ingredients that don’t require as much water as the other ingredients. 

I wonder why chicken continues to increase in people’s diets throughout every year. I also wonder why beef requires the most water out of other ingredients.

These graphs relate to me and my community because in America fast food places are everywhere and mostly everyone in my community consumes fast food. This would mean that big amounts of water would continue to be used for fast food places instead of being reserved for my community. Including the fact that fast food restaurants infect our communities' diets and health.

A title I would make for this article would be “ America's Fast Food Restaurants: Disrupted Diets and Water Usage”

I notice that beef and pork consumption has remained stable for the most part since 1920, while chicken consumption has surged, surpassing peaks in both beef and pork consumption. Being that chicken has become a dietary staple for Americans, rising in popularity recently. The other graph shows that chicken requires significantly less water compared to beef, indicating a shift from beef to chicken could positively impact water consumption. The reasons behind chicken's popularity and beef's decline since the late 70s concern me and my community due to the pressing water scarcity issue in many regions.

Poultry Prevails!

raw_comment:
- I noticed that chicken consumption makes up most of American diet, with beef and pork coming second and third. I also notice that chicken consumption per person has been increasing since 1920, while beef and pork consumption seem to have decreased almost 60 years after 1920. 
- I wonder what the cause for the drop in beef and pork consumption was, and why they did not continue an increasing trend like chicken. 
- This relates to my community because chicken seems to be a popular meat used in several styles of cooking. Beef and pork are also known to not be eaten by some due to religion, so chicken seems to be a mostly universal meat to eat. 
- Meet the Rise in Meat

raw_comment:
I noticed that the most consumed food by Americans today is chicken, and beef comes in as second. The lowest consumed food (on the graph) today is yogurt, which has gained much traction compared to its absence in the 1960s. While chicken has been on a rather steady rise for decades, beef was actually consumed far more than chicken in the 1970s, but quickly declined and was surpassed by chicken in the 1990s.

I wonder why the consumption of beef has declined so much since the 1970s, and why Americans have been consuming chicken more and more. Could it be due to vegetarian movements, or simply resource costs? Is it because chicken takes less time to cultivate and requires less resources, like the groundwater usage in the second graph(therefore also being cheaper)?

It’s interesting how much chicken and beef have become a staple in the American diet. The amount of water being used can also be concerning, as water is also a vital resource for many energy processes, and basic human survival and necessities. This raises awareness for where the foods from our diets come from and how much it costs to create them.

raw_comment:
1.)  I noticed that since the early 1900s, the American diet has changed to include increasingly more chicken and cheese. As time increased and groundwater levels decreased, diets were comprised of more chicken and cheese. This may be because the cost of water in beef is 2,110 gallons of water per pound. As a result, producers may be drawn towards a more cost-efficient alternative, which would be the production of chicken, costing 410 gallons of water per pound instead. With more more producers, the cost of chicken would decrease, causing more consumers to buy it, and therefore explaining the increasing prominence of chicken in American diets. 
2.) I wonder why beef costs 2,110 gallons of water per pound to produce. Even though chicken and cheese saw a increase in popularity in American diets, beef and pork stayed relatively the same. However, when looking at the cost of water for both products, the cost of water in beef outsized that of the pork’s by a wide margin. 
3.) This relates to me and my community since this reflects the the prominence of certain foods in diets and their costs. The awareness of the costs of popular foods in American diets can help promote better decisions that are less costly for families. 
4.) An Overview of Popular Foods in American Diets and their  Water Costs

1. I notice from the second graph that beef is by far the leading factor for water consumption in the food and agricultural industry. The other meats like pork and cheese both invoke a mid-range decline in groundwater. I also noticed on the first graph that chicken has experienced a steady increase in the American diet. raw_comment:
1. Both beef and pork used to make up a larger percentage of the average American's diet than chicken, but that has changed over the years. In ~1982, chicken surpassed pork, and in ~1991, chicken surpassed beef. As of 2020, chicken makes up slightly less than pork and beef combined. Also, chicken costs less water to produce than beef or pork.

2. I wonder why yogurt seemed nonexistent in peoples' diets until ~1960

3. This relates to my community because chicken is a very popular food with many people that I know, which is a better alternative than a beef popularity, which would be costly in water.

4. "Times are changing, and diets with it- what a water shortage could mean for these popular foods."

My headline would be "eating chicken everyday, keeps the water in the bay."

raw_comment: According to figure 1, over the last 100 years, chicken consumption has increased exponentially. Other products like cheese and yogurt have followed this pattern as well, but not as significantly as chicken. Beef and pork consumption has more or less stayed the same. raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
In the graph titled, "Americans' Changing Diet," chicken and cheese are rising in popularity in the United States. Yogurt has also been increasing, but to a lesser extent. On the other hand, beef and pork are declining in terms of their consumption. In the graph titled, "The Cost in Water of Some Popular Foods," beef overwhelmingly surpasses the other foods. The usage of cows for food seems to have a dire financial consequence with beef and cheese being amongst the most expensive to produce. 

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what caused chicken and cheese to soar in popularity. I am also curious about whether this increase can be attributed to influence from other cuisines. Additionally, I am fascinated that chicken has less of a cost despite it being widely consumed. 

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This connects to me and my community since I tend to avoid red meat in my diet. However, I do consume dairy in the forms of yogurt and cheese quite frequently. I find it interesting to learn more about the finances involved in creating such products. 

4. Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.

"Land of the Free? More like Land of the Chicken and Cheese."

raw_comment:
1. I see that since 1960, Americans have been eating more and more chicken going up to the present day. While this is happening, beef and pork diets have been relatively constant. A small increase of cheese/yogurt is also present. 

2. I am mainly wondering why chicken started to skyrocket in consumption compared to beef/pork. The second graph shows that the cost in water may play a role with beef, as it costs by far the most per pound, of over 2100 gallons required. However, Pork and Chicken are relatively the same, only being a 80 gallon or 17% difference. The reason why pork stayed constant and chicken increased is not able to be concluded with this graph.

3. This relates to me as it takes place in the present day. The data on the graph is still ongoing, and seeing that chicken has the highest consumption also means that chickens out of all of the meats shown (especially cause chickens are smaller than pigs/cows) needs to be bred the most. Its highly probable that there's a point where chicken consumption out weighs this, and the supply will decrease leading to higher prices. 

4. A title that I am thinking of could be "How America's diet helps/hurts the environment."

1.) What do you notice?
The first graph illustrates the significant rise of the consumption of chicken as well as cheese. Beef and pork are also rising although they both fell from their peak consumption. Additionally, yogurt is making a steady climb to almost 20 pounds per person. Chicken and cheese also have a lower water need in comparison to other foods, especially beef as it requires 2110 gallons of water per pound in comparison to just the 520 gallons for cheese and 410 gallons for chicken.

2.) What do you wonder?
I wonder if the amount of food Americans consume, not just what type, is also shifting. I also wonder what caused the large rise of popularity in chicken in comparison to other types of meat. There may be a relation between the type of food consumed, and the amount of water it needs.

In terms of my community, it could affect the types of food we have access to since the amount of water being used is trending upwards. This, in turn, could negatively affect us as many depend on chicken, cheese, and other such products as a main source of nutrition. 

4.) Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.
“Ever wonder just how much water we use for our food? It’s more than you may think.”

raw_comment:
Chicken and Processed Food?

It's fairly interesting to see Chicken become a larger part of the average American's diet, while more red meats such as Pork continue to decline in overall usage. Cheese and Yogurt, which can both be easily found in grocery stores and in processed foods, are also increasing as parts of the average American's diet. It's likely that the rate at which chicken is being adopted as part of the American diet is greater than the rate at which red meats are being let go from diets, as water usage continues to drop significantly, yet red meats require more water consumption than chicken. As processed food and obesity become more common throughout America, it's vital for people to consider how we can change the overall American's diet in a healthier way while being climate-healthy in a world worsening with climate change.

raw_comment: Americans eat such an unsustainable diet it’s insane how nobody does anything to change this. Have you ever walked into the average public school cafeteria. Every single meal has either pork, beef, or chicken as the main source of protein and calories. This needs to change. Not only is meat not healthy for people in the long run, the quality of life of these animals is absolutely terrible. Factory farming is a disgusting way to treat living creatures. We stuff them in tight cages and inject them with hormones and antibiotics that end up in the food we feed our children. And these staple meats aren’t good for the environment either. The demand for cheap, mass produced chicken, beef and pork had pit a strain on our natural environment: It drains groundwater leaving the soil stripped of nutrients, pollutes nearby water sources and spreads disease among animals and humans. The healthier, more sustainable, and more humane alternative is to cut back on the meat. I understand completely eliminating meat from the American diet is impossible, but nobody even tries to look for moderation. There doesn’t need to be one or the other, balance is what we must strive for.

raw_comment:
The amount of chicken that Americans eat has increased tremendously. I am surprised to see that beef and pork are eaten less than chicken. I thought chicken would require more water as it is commonly eaten by Americans. Lentils, beans, and green peas require less water than the meats which is surprising. Dairy such as cheese and yogurt are not as popular as beef, pork, and chicken. Lastly, popular foods of Americans’ changing diet require a lot of water.

Why do cheese and yogurt require less water? If most individuals switch to a vegetarian diet, how would this affect the cost in water of popular foods? What foods would become more popular?  If Americans stopped consuming meat, how would this impact the environment?  What can humans eat that does not require a lot of water? If humans continue overconsuming meat, what will happen to the environment in 2060? How much water is needed to produce fish? 

This relates to me as I am a meat-eater and enjoy burgers, steak, and chicken. However, may be best to consume less meat and eat foods that require less water in order to help the planet.  It was interesting to look at food from the perspective of production as I did not know that large amounts of water are used to produce common foods. Water is important, not only for drinking, but also for the production and growing of foods, so it should be conserved as much as possible.

Chicken Is Bacon the World Crazy

raw_comment:
When looking at this graph I notice that chicken is currently the number one choice of meat for Americans. The second and third choice is beef and pork, Over the years chicken has risen into the diet of many Americans but it was not always like this. For example, during the 1980's, beef was the main thing in the diets of Americans but it has decreased and chicken has increased. Cheese has also made its way into peoples diets, it was at the bottom but over the years it has risen slowly.  In the second graph I notice that beef uses the most water to produce and this makes sense because in order to get meat you must first raise and feed the cow which uses a lot of water because cows drink a lot. 

I wonder how yogurt is so low in the first graph, I also wonder how almonds require so much water to be produced in the second graph. 

This relates to my community because it shows how much we rely on these meats, we as Americans don't want to eat anything else and in the future this could impact us negatively. 

A heading- "Americans, food, and water"

raw_comment:
I notice that the consumption of chicken in Americans' diets has for the most part increased at a steady rate for the past one hundred years. I notice that it does not cost much water to produce chicken in comparison to beef. I wonder if the reason it has always been so prominent in Americans' diets is because it does not cost so much water to be produced. I wonder if the fact that beef costs 2,110 gallons of water to produce is the reason why Americans' diets included less of it, especially more recently. This could also be a factor in why beef is more expensive than chicken. This decrease in meat consumption in Americans' diets could have also been caused by the increase in vegetarians and vegans in the more recent decades. People have become more environmentally cautious and aware lately and this impacts people's consumption of food and also government policies that could affect the sale and production of food. This relates to myself and my community as I along with my family and friends consume all of the items on this graph. In fact, I probably do consume chicken the most and yogurt the least.
Food Frenzy!

raw_comment:
The first graph shows how America's diet has changed from 1920-2020. This graph tracks various produce (chicken, yogurt, beef, pork, and cheese) in terms of pounds per person. The second graph tracks how much water it takes to produce these foods. The first graph shows the popularity of chicken has skyrocketed from under 20 pounds per person in the 1920s to over 80 pounds per person in 2020. It can be concluded this is because farming chickens takes up less water that other meats such as pork and beef as shown in the second graph. In the past few decades, Americans have become more aware of environmental concerns. There is a direct correlation between this new ideology and the increasing popularity of chicken. As Americans aim to conserve water, they are producing more chicken rather than beef and pork because it takes up less water. Cheese is another product that has become popular. I wonder why cheese takes up so much less water to produce than beef if they come from the same animal (cows). I also wondered why yogurt only began gaining popularity in the 1960's. The internet said yogurt only began being sold in America in 1942. In the 1950s, yogurt began gaining popularity because it was ruled a "health food". This graph relates to me because these products have extremely high water consumption which has detrimental effects on the environment. The longer we ignore this damage for the profits of large businesses, the worse this issue is going to get. 
"Foods vs. Facts"

raw_comment: The upward trend of chicken consumption is to be expected, as it is the cheapest and most available meat in America. Something notable is the decrease in the popularity of beef, which could be due to red meat falling out of favor with health professionals for its role in America's heart disease crisis. Despite beef's decline, other cattle products such as cheese and yogurt have been growing in popularity, which is a natural result of the growth of the dairy industry. Overall, the trends in the popularity of beef and chicken indicate that our diet will become more sustainable as time continues. However, the seemingly positive trend must be considered alongside the growing population, which will continue to put more strain on the meat industry and overall increase water expenditure. You could name the graph: "The Fowl Cost for Water".

1. I noticed that chicken wasn't as popular as I thought it was going to be in the 1950s, but beef and pork were instead, i always thought the chicken was always the most popular.

2. I wonder if the chicken will eventually drop down in popularity because of the amount of water used for soybeans, and if Yorgert will grow higher since it seems to be slowly growing but not as high as the other animal products, maybe it could have a high spike in the future?

3.  This is related to me and my community since the majority of our preferred diet consists of animal products which could affect the environment with the amount of water used. I think we need other alternatives to our diet like eating more beans and green peas since they use less water, and the resources used to make the food for the animals as well since popularity is quickly going up.

4. The diets preferred by Americans and the consequences.

raw_comment:
I notice that since 1920, chicken has risen as being the most consumed meat, compared to beef and pork which either decreased or stayed consistent. In addition, chicken is the meat with the least amount of water per pound, which most likely contributes to the increase in consumption. 
Why has the consumption of cheese also risen even though it is in the top three cost in water? What other factors play into this? 
This relates to my community as these foods are some of the most popular. My family consumes these foods and also my school dining services provide these foods often for lunch. 
"Chicken Tenders or Life?"

raw_comment:
This graph, and its supporting graph, shows the rise of food production and how this food is starting to affect groundwater. Chicken consumption, for example, has drastically increased for the average American person. However, chickens, before they are killed for food, are fed by soybeans. The amount of soybean having to be produced has hurt the groundwater supply across states like Arkansas. In all, chicken production has an intake of 410 gallons of water per pound. I wonder if the production and consumption of chicken keeps rising, like it has been since the 1940s, how will this continue to negatively impact places such as Arkansas? Is there a time when their groundwater supply may run out? In my community, most people eat organic foods and meat, which is better for the environment. While our consumption harms the groundwater supply, it is better for the environment in terms of less gas release and waste management. 
“Are Chickens Stealing Our Water?”

raw_comment:
1) I noticed chicken has taken over the American diet with cheese quickly catching up. Since 1920, the consumption of chicken has increased significantly, surpassing the consumption of other meats such as beef and pork. Cheese is also steadily increasing.

2) I wonder how the growth in consumption of chicken and cheese will affect the already declining groundwater as both are steadily increasing and cost a lot of water, with cheese costing 520 gallons per pound and chicken 410 gallons per pound. 

3) It relates to me and my community because we are the ones consuming these products and contributing to this growth. The more people consume these products, the more we are draining the earth's groundwater, which poses a huge threat to the environment and possibly our future survival.

4) American Diet, Declining Water Levels

raw_comment:
Why Did the Chicken Cross the Road? To Get Onto Americans’ Plates

I notice that while the amount of beef and pork that Americans eat tends to fluctuate over the course of 100 years, the amount of chicken, cheese, and yogurt seems to progressively increase over the years. I notice that Americans’ tendency to eat more chicken in comparison to beef is beneficial to the environment considering that beef requires approximately 5x as much water per pound than chicken. I also notice that almonds require a significant amount of water per pound. I was surprised that almonds use up 560 gallons of water per pound and this data point can also be used to amplify how much water is required in beef as beef still requires 4x as much water as almonds. 

I wonder why Americans tend to consume more chicken than beef and pork. Is it due to differences in cost, health reasons, or just preference in taste? I wonder why beef requires such a significant amount of water per pound. I also wonder if there really is any correlation between the cost in water of these foods in relation to their popularity in Americans’ diets.

raw_comment: What do you notice?I noticed that chicken has had a steady incline of pounds per person from 1920-2020 with an almost 100lbs incline in pounds per person. I also noticed that beef reached its height during the late 1970s and early 1980s. Pork reached its height between 1940-1960. What do you wonder? I wonder why chicken has had such an increase since 1920 because it is more environmentally friendly. I also wonder if since pork and beef had a different peak, were they used as substitutes for each other? Title:Don't keep America beefy.

raw_comment: The graph depicts the changing diets of the American population. Since 1920, the consumption of chicken, cheese, and yogurt has greatly increased. On the other hand, the consumption of beef and pork has fluctuated significantly. Chicken requires 410 gallons of water per pound, whereas beef requires 2,110 gallons of water per pound. This means that the consumption of chicken is good for the environment, in comparison to the consumption of beef. I wonder what has impacted the trends behind this graph. What caused chicken to become more prominent in people’s diets? This relates to my community because I eat the foods shown on the graph. Additionally, the price of these goods in comparison to their supply and demand impact the community. I would title this graph: “The Fluctuating American Diets.”

raw_comment:
I notice that Americans' consumption of chicken and cheese has increased significantly since 1960. Chicken has even exceeded the consumption of beef in the 1980s (90lb per person), indicating a dramatic shift in Americans' diet. This is good for the environment because beef requires 2,110 gallons of water per pound compared to 410 for chicken.

I wonder why chicken and cheese began increasing in the 1960s. I imagine that the environmental movements of the time precipitated the change, though it is less clear why yogurt gained popularity. I also wonder how Americans' overall health correlates with this graph. Is fast food factored in?

This affects my community because we are arriving at a water crisis. The description suggests that even the production of feed for chickens is depleting aquifers, so we may need to find a less water-intensive dietary alternative. I try to eat more chicken myself to avoid the water-intense beef.

This graph depicts the changes in Americans' diets and food items' water consumption. 

"Foodies' Favorites Shift"

raw_comment:
In these graphs, we see the changing diet of American citizens since 1920, as well as the water cost for the items on the list. Over the years we notice chicken increasing the most, and yogurt remaining close to the bottom from start to finish on the first graph. It is interesting that on the other graph, chicken only has 410 gallons per pound, while on the other hand, beef has over 2,000. The other two types of meat on the first graph, beef and pork, are also relatively highly consumed for the entirety of the graph. Consumption of cheese has increased every year on the graph, so I wonder what this graph will look like years from now. Will the continuously increasing lines keep rising or will they begin decreasing? I also wonder if the reason the meats seem to be decreasing in more recent years is that more people might be becoming vegan/vegetarian as that is becoming more popular in society. I also wonder if it has to do with the fact that the gallons of water per pound is significantly more for beef than chicken or pork. This relates to me and my community because I, too, am a consumer of the foods on the graph. My diet and what I consume is part of what the first graph is all about. 

"Don't Chicken Out of a Good Diet!"

I notice that chicken and cheese have increased the most in the past decades. Compared to beef, pork, and yogurt. I wonder why chickens have grown so much. Is it because it's cheaper or healthier? Personally, I'd rather have beef. The graph also shows how beef and cheese take up a lot of water costs. Is this because of how much water cows drink? I wonder if this affects the accessibility to these things, making them less popular. This relates to my community because I've seen chicken become a more prevalent thing in my life, and I only eat beef on special occasions. It can affect my community as well because cheese isn't necessarily healthy, and could impact the health of people around the country.

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph depicts American citizens changing their diet over time from 1920-2020. I notice that Americans have been consuming more chicken than beef these past years. The question posed at the top of the graph is how the foods, chicken, beef, pork, cheese, and yogurt affect the environment which is something I've never thought about but it's intriguing. The second graph below compares American's diet and favorite foods to the amount of water needed to produce a pound of these products. Beef takes up the most water while chicken is the lowest amount of water -- doesn't need as much. I wonder why Americans love their chicken compared to other foods since beef was more popular in past years. Could that be because chicken uses way less water which is more beneficial to the environment? I wonder if the pounds of beef per person, which is 2,100 has decreased because the price of water is high which leads to less production and consumers. This relates to my community because I love chicken and eat it a lot and I have noticed the inflation of food prices in chicken and strawberries or everything at the supermarkets. It's tough out here with the inflation rates as my mom refuses to buy me $9 strawberries LOL. Also, I have seen diet changes through the media such as vegan, paleo, gluten-free, etc. Most people are vegan for ethical reasons to protect the environment. 

Clean, Green, Lean Diet

raw_comment:
What do you notice? In Graph 1, " Americans' Changing Diet ", it shows specific food products and how many pounds of these products are eaten every year per American. Chicken and cheese have had a steady increase in popularity since 1920, and have continued to climb until the present.
In Graph 2, " The Cost in Water of Some Popular Foods ", it shows how many gallons of water are used to produce one pound of some popular foods. Beef is the most draining of all, consuming 2,110 gallons per pound. Cheese and chicken are more moderate in their consumption, with chicken using 410 gallons per pound and cheese using 520 gallons per pound, respectively.
I wonder why Graph 2 specifically matters. Doesn't water go back into the environment anyway? Just because water is used in the production of something, that doesn't mean that it just disappears from the water cycle forever. Maybe the water is contaminated? I'm not sure.
This relates to me and my community because I eat most of these products and so do the people around me. Other than that I don't see the significance or how it applies to me.

raw_comment: In the first graph, it is measuring the change in Americans’ diets from around 1920 to 2020 by the amount of pounds of different food items eaten per person. I noticed that in 2020, the most eaten food item was chicken, surpassing 80 pounds per person, whereas the least eaten item was yogurt at around 15 pounds per person. I wonder why chicken was the most eaten by Americans in 2020 and what caused there to be such a great spike in pounds per person over the years. Additionally, I noticed that there was a peak in beef intake around 1980, but it started to decrease again in the following years. In the second graph, it depicts the cost in water of certain foods. I noticed that beef had the highest cost of water of 2,110. Connecting to the first graph, I wonder if the pounds of beef per person has seen a trend of decrease since 1980 because it requires so much water and the cost is so high, leading to less production and available beef to consumers. I also wonder if there have been any recent efforts to try to reduce the water amount and cost to produce foods like beef and almonds. This relates to my community because I have noticed food prices constantly fluctuating, with a trend of them mainly increasing, and have witnessed changes in people’s diets based on certain trends in society. My headline for this graph would be: “What You Consume is Not Just Food but a Catalyst for Environmental Change”.

raw_comment:
From the first graph, I noticed that Americans in 2020 favor chicken the most, then beef, pork, cheese, and yogurt. The popularity of chicken and cheese in Americans’ diet has been in a steady increase since 1920, but the amount of beef and pork eaten has fluctuated. In the second graph, I noticed that beef requires the highest cost in water at 2,110 gallons of water per pound. I wonder how much the graphs impact one another. Specifically, I wonder how the decline in Americans’ consumption of beef since 1980 has impacted the environment. Will beef’s “water footprint” in America also decline? Due to this, is it beneficial that Americans are consuming more pounds of chicken (as 520 gallons of water are necessary per pound compared to beef’s 2,110)? How do food-production industries and farms in the United States deal with the changing diets of Americans’ and the amount of water used? The graphs relate to me because I, along with other Americans, consume a greater amount of chicken than beef and pork. This change in Americans’ diet over the years, can impact my community and its environment due to the amount of water required per pound. 

"Chick-Out The Impact of Americans’ Diet”

raw_comment:
I notice that Americans have begun consuming more chicken than beef in the 20 years. This consequently is better for the environment, more specifically the water levels. Beef takes up the most water, meanwhile, chicken is the lowest amount of water needed on the list. 
 I wonder if this trend of chicken being the most consumed will continue, or a new craze will emerge, and beef will go back to the top.
 This relates to me and my community because if we continue this trend, we may be able to make a huge difference, especially since the over population of cows are bad for environment due to their release of methane.
 A possible headline could be "Chickens are helping the environment!"

raw_comment: This graph examines the eating habits of Americans over the last 100 years. It then use another graph to compare American's diet and favorite foods to the amount of water needed to produce a pound of these products. The amounts and popularity of the food in Graph One align pretty well with what I would expect based on my knowledge of the American diet. It is, however, disappointing and concerning how this graph lacks any fruits, vegetables, and produce, which are vital to a healthy diet. I was surprised by the amount of water it takes to produce one pound of each product, the number seems so large I cannot imagine how that amount is necessary. These graphs are concerning to me because of the lack of healthy foods being consumed and the excessive amounts of water used to produce them. I think the large consumption of water used to produce these products is alarming, knowing the limited amounts of fresh water that are available across the globe. I would title these graphs "How is the Average American's Diet Impacting the World?"

raw_comment:
What I notice is that both Chicken and cheese have become one of the most prevalent foods within American’s daily diets. Over the last 100 years, chicken has increased the most out of any other food, like beef, pork, cheese, and yogurt. 

What I wonder is what made chicken become so popular in America's diets that it rose to that level? Do chicken nuggets truly have that big of an impact? 

What’s going on in this graph is it is not only trying to show how Chicken has grown immensely in popularity but how beef and cheese take up a huge percentage of the cost in water. Since cows require so much water in order to sustain their health, a large amount of it goes towards that industry and is immensely affecting the environment. 

This relates to my community because I believe that I have seen chicken, pork, and cheese become a huge part of many peoples diets that I know, including my own. Especially things like cheese pizza and chicken nuggets are good alternatives for picky eaters, so I see that as a big draw as a meal for many people I know.

raw_comment:
We have two titles: 1) “We have beef with beef” and 2)“Don’t forget about yogurt.”
We noticed that the two that are increasing a lot over time are chicken and cheese. Around 1980, there was a heavy spike in beef, and a decrease in pork.Between 2000 and 2010, there was a decrease in beef and pork at the same time. Chicken consumption still steadily increased during this time. Cheese increase is not volatile - the growth is more stable. Yogurt only shows up on the graph from the 1970s. Beef costs significantly more in water than any other meat. Almonds require an exceptionally high amount of water.
We wonder how much water does it take to raise rice? Why does beef take so much water? How were these numbers calculated? Does the water cost for raising beef include growing the food for the cows? Does the calculation include transporting the food from farm to table? Does the introduction of fast food brands have anything to do with these trends? Why is there such an increase in chicken? In the Netherlands, we eat a lot of cheese, so the water cost of dairy is important.

raw_comment:
We noticed that, over time, there has been a steady increase in the consumption of chicken and cheese in the U.S. We noticed the consumption is based on a 5-year rolling average. The consumption of beef decreased after 1980, so it no longer the most popular. The decrease in beef consumption is good because beef uses a lot of water.

We wonder if beef consumption has decreased because of the amount of water needed, inflation, or health reasons. Does cost play a role in the increase in chicken? We also wonder why chicken and cheese are highlighted in color.
We are not in the U.S., so would we see similar patterns in Europe?

It still impacts our community because our food choices affect the environment.

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that between the 1920s and the 2020s, American's preferences for cheese, yogurt, and chicken seem to have grown, but their tastes for beef and pork have been relatively stable. It's clear that Americans eat the most chicken and the least yogurt. I also noticed that producing beef uses the greatest water.

2) I wonder why even though yogurt is healthier than chicken, it is the food that is eaten the least. I also wonder why even if all three varieties of meat are the same, why the rate of pork and beef has been the same while the rate of chicken has climbed significantly? I wonder why Chicken is so much higher than Beef - I think the decrease in Beef around 1980 could potentially be a point in time when Americans became aware of the health risks associated with red meat. 

This relates to me and my community because I have personally noticed a lot more people I know, whether friends or classmates, have more recently become vegetarian. In my family, majority of the people are already vegetarian, so our consumption of meat varies greatly from this graph. 

A catchy title could be "Winner Winner, Chicken Dinner"

2. I wonder what could have caused the disparity between chicken consumption and the consumption of other meats. I theorize that it could be due to the cost of production of chicken when compared to other meats, or potentially a more health conscious public.
3. I think this graph displays a trend that I have noticed in my community. Recently I have noticed that more restaurants and cafeterias have been serving dishes that feature chicken as the main source of protein more often.
4. Food and Water Always Go Together

1. What I see from the graph is that the American diet has changed dramatically. For example, in 1920, chicken was one of the least consumed foods, whereas it is currently the most consumed food. I also see a rise in consumer demand for cheese and yogurt. While Beef and pork have remained consistent. However, overall chicken is the most consumed, while yogurt is the least. I also found that meat has the highest water content, whereas green peas are the lowest. 
2. I wonder what factors have caused these changes in America’s diet? I also wonder why beef costs so much in water?
3. This affects me and the community I live in since hamburgers, pizza, and chicken nuggets are frequently consumed, and as a result, these foods are produced more for the public to purchase, impacting local groundwater resources. 
4. "The Truth About America's Favorite Foods."

raw_comment:
I notice that while chicken is the most consumed food today in the American diet (this number has been increasing since 1920), the decline in groundwater that matches chicken is 410, which is in the middle of the popular foods that are consumed. 

I wonder why yogurt was not consumed until the 1970's? Is it because it could not be safely preserved and manufactured? In addition, I wonder if the reason beef consumption has decreased over the past decade is because it uses 2110 gallons of water per pound?

This relates to my community because it gives us valuable information on what we can do collectively to be more conservative and make better choices for our planet. For instance, the graph shows us that beef uses 2110 gallons of water per pound, and we can be more eco friendly by consuming less beef.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the American diet has changed drastically since the 1920s, with their chicken consumption increasing over 4x. Additionally, I noticed that beef consumption largely increased during the 1960-1980 only to drop back down. 
2. I wonder what made Americans change their diet to chicken so much. Paired with the other chart, I wonder if it is because chicken is cheaper by the pound than other forms of meat, considering that beef costs over 2,000 gallons of water per pound. 
3. This relates to me and my community because we all buy food from grocery stores and eat different types of food, so we should be aware of how much it costs. The supply and demand of food constantly causes prices to change, so if we are aware of which foods are more popular, it allows us to be aware of the cost. Plus, knowing about the food we have reminds us how lucky we are to have such easy access to the food we need. 
4. A catchy headline could be: What’s on your plate?

1) I notice that according to the first graph, chicken has become a major part of many Americans' diets over the years. Since the beginning of the graph, chicken started as one of the least part of American diets, and it has increased over the years, leading since around 1980. Yet, from 1990-2020, cheese and chicken demonstrated an increase, with chicken skyrocketing from going below 20 pounds in 1920 to above 80 pounds in 2020. How will the decay of groundwater levels, slow down other aspects and necessities for Americans and our environment?
3) This relates to my community and me as chicken and cheese are the most commonly used foods to cook/prep daily meals, meaning that my community constantly contributes these foods to their diets which affects the groundwater levels. 
4) American Diets Are Draining Groundwater Levels!

raw_comment:
The graph illustrates a significant increase in consumption of cheese and chicken, with chicken experiencing a particularly steep rise compared to other foods. This suggests a shift in dietary preferences, with cheese and chicken becoming more popular among Americans. On the other hand, pork and beef seem to have experienced a decline in popularity. I wonder if religious preferences, such as kosher Jews' tendency to avoid pork, play a role in this data. I also wonder why beef was so high close to the 1980s and had dropped significantly within the past 40 years. This relates to me and my community with chicken being the most popular on this list because in my diet I tend to stay away from all meat except chicken.

raw_comment:
We noticed that both of these graphs are investigating water use in relation to food production. In both graphs, cheese and chicken are different colors, and we wonder why those are being highlighted. Also we noticed that the first graph only lists 5 foods, while the second lists 9. The first graph also has a time span, but the second does not, and the graphs are from different sources. Yogurt is included only on the first graph. Why are chicken and cheese highlighted? Why does beef take so much more water than any other category? Are they trying to highlight the rise of chicken and cheese? For the first graph, is it pound per person per year? 

We all eat these foods, and even though water is plentiful in The Netherlands,  we recognize that in other places, water is scarce and that the items could end up costing more if we don’t manage our resources.  

We would title this story “The Cost of Water in the American Diet.”

raw_comment:
I notice that chicken is the most popular food in the American diet and people are eating it more now than ever before. Chicken surpasses beef which was the most popular food between 1920 and 1980 after it overtook pork around 1960.

I wonder whether quality, quantity, or simply preference is attributing to the rise in people eating chicken. I also wonder how the data is being collected because certain areas in the US might prefer certain foods over others.

This relates to me and my community because food prices and preferences are constantly changing which means markets and food outlets must change due to demand from the public.

More Chicken?

raw_comment:
I've noticed that the amount of food consumed per person has been steadily increasing for things like chicken, cheese, and yogurt, but has been declining for goods like beef and pork. 
I'm curious how these figures would change if the research included fake or substitute forms of these items, or whether they are currently included. How, for instance, would cheese consumption alter if cheese analogs—which many with dietary restrictions enjoy—were included? Furthermore, what effect would this have on water prices?
This is relevant to our community since I've been noticing how much cheese and chicken I've been eating lately. The availability of these well-liked products may be the reason behind this. I also include these things in a lot of my meals.
The Evolution Of Our Diet

For example, we have noticed that the amount of chicken that is being eaten has increased exponentially over time. As a group, we were wondering if it is due to chickens being more profitable, more available, tastier, healthier, and/or cheaper. We believe the largest factor for the increase in chicken consumption is the low price of chicken compared to the price of other products on the graph.

In conclusion, there are a few different variables that could affect the increase in chicken consumption. Because of this, it is hard to be certain from this graph of the possible variables that affect the change in chicken consumption the most.

raw_comment: The What’s Going On in This Graph? March 6, 2024 was based upon food. We ended up with the title “Old McDonalds Diet”. We noticed that the colors of the bars were McDonald-based. The meats are consumed the most out of everything else. We also noticed that the lines for meat on the graph ended above the lines for cheese and yogurt. The chicken, specifically, was the most consumed meat. Based on our observations we had many different questions. The things we specifically wondered 3 different things. What happened to make chicken shoot up in the graph? Does “cost in water” imply the amount of water needed to make the food? How are eggs and chicken different for the cost of water? The second graph talks about “The cost in water of some popular foods” and sheds light on the environmental impacts of certain foods. Many people don’t usually ponder how much water is used to bring about their ingredients. This could reveal to my community how much of a certain food we eat, which may be more than some would consider healthy.

While looking at the graphs, I noticed that American's love for chicken, cheese, and yogurt have increased from the 1920s to the 2020s, whereas the love for beef and pork remained somewhat constant. Chicken is clearly the most consumed food by Americans and yogurt is the least. I also noticed that beef consumes the most water to produce.

raw_comment:
I noticed that beef requires significantly more water per pound to produce. I also noticed that vegetables (such as beans, lentils, and peas) require a lot less water per pound than beef. 
I wonder how this can disproportionately affect farming communities that produce beef or almonds for example. I also wonder about the distribution of water, for example, how much water is used to feed the animals vs produce the meat. 
This relates to me because my family and I mostly eat vegetarian. It puts into perspective the effects of eating meat on the environment
A title could be “Effects of Popular Foods on Water”

raw_comment:
I notice that while foods such as beef and pork have continued to remain relatively steady in their consumption per person, chicken, cheese and yogurt have been on the rise. 

Something I wonder is how these numbers would fluctuate if artificial versions / alternative versions of these foods were included in the study (or if they are already included). For example, how would the consumption of cheese change if cheese analogue was included (which many with dietary restrictions like). Additionally, how would this impact the cost of water?

This relates to me and my community because these foods are readily available for consumption and it is important to consider the cost in water that these products might have.

raw_comment:
I noticed that chicken along with cheese has gained more popularity as time progressed. On the other hand, it is displayed by the first graph that beef and pork started to gain, but then lost their popularity since the 1920's until now. 

I wonder why chicken specifically has gained more popularity than beef and pork; what attracts people more to chicken than to beef or pork? I also wonder what caused Americans to add more cheese into their diets since it has increased significantly in popularity. 

This relates to me and my community as these are all food items that most people consume. Our eating habits influence the graphs depicted. 

A catchy headline could be: "Chicken and Cheese Seem to Please."

We notice that chicken has become the most consumed edible animal product over the decades, beating out pork and beef which had major declines since their peak consumption around 1940 (pork) and 1980 (beef). Almost 100 pounds of chicken is consumed per person per year as of 2020. Less than 60 pounds of pork and beef are consumed per person per year as of 2020. In the second graph, beef costs more than triple the amount of water than any other food listed.

We wonder why certain foods require the amount of water they need, such as beef requiring 2,110 gallons versus almonds needing 500 gallons per pound in 2019. We also wonder what caused products like chicken and cheese to see significant increases in consumption over 100 years while pork and beef decreased largely.

This relates to our community because I've noticed how much chicken and cheese specifically I have eaten recently. This might be attributed to the availability of these popular items. These foods are also part of many of the meals I eat.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that chicken is the most popular food in an American's changing diet as of 2020, and had a sharp incline since 1940. Yogurt is the least popular food, and only gained interest in 1960. I also noticed that beef and almonds have the highest water cost.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why the cost of water for beef is so high. I also wonder if Americans' love for foods will continue increasing as the years go on, and if they already have, and how badly the groundwater levels are being affected. I also wonder how the decrease of groundwater levels will affect our eating habits and make it harder to grow food.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because all people eat foods that have water in them because it’s a part of your daily diet. It’s also really hard for people to stop eating foods like chicken, beef, and cheese because people love them and don’t want to let them go.

raw_comment:
We notice that demand for chicken is increasing, and as is it's cost in water, which is a concerning figure. We also noticed that beef is extremely costly in water, and although its demand is declining, the disproportionate amount of water that it needs makes beef a bad environmental choice.

We wonder why the demand for beef and pork is decreasing while chicken is dramatically increasing. We also wonder if the decreased space that almonds need to be produced in comparison to other products counteracts the amount of water that they need to grow, making it a potentially environmentally sound decision in comparison to other meat and dairy products.

This relates to our community because we all eat and have to make decisions on which foods we'd prefer to eat for a variety of reasons: dietary, preference-based, religious, and environmental concerns. These graphs can help inform people on the food consumption trends and the environmental costs of these foods, leading people to choose for themselves what they want to eat.

A possible headline for this graph could be "Chicken Chicken Chicken... Who's Water Bill are You Paying?

raw_comment: There is a little bit of information missing about the first graph, namely the duration in time for each contributing data point. I will assume it is the annual consumption of each staple in pounds per person. The line is a running average over five years, which smooths it out a bit and makes it easier to see long term trends. Chicken, cheese, and yogurt have gone up a lot but beef and pork have not declined nearly as much, in other words, it looks like people are either many more pounds of these protein-rich staples per year nowadays than earlier. I wonder if there are other staples, not on this graph, that have significant reductions in consumption. If not, this graph implies that the number of calories that people consume has gone up significantly and if that is the case, this graph may show a nice correlation with mean weight, or BMI, of the population over time. If there are other staples that people eat significantly less of, it would be interesting to know what their water needs are. Also, the first graph is per person, which is great, but the population has also increased. So not only has this protein intake increased per person but even more so on an absolute scale because population has increased. Lots of interesting questions to ask about these data and what the implications are!

- **Top:** Multi-series **line chart**
- **Bottom:** **Horizontal bar chart**

## 2) Layout techniques
- The visualization is a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** multiple lines overlaid in a single plot (not faceted, not stacked).
- **Bottom panel:** a single horizontal bar chart (not faceted, not stacked).
- Color is used to highlight selected food categories across both panels.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top line chart) |
| Pounds per person | Quantitative | Position on y-axis (top line chart) |
| Food category (Chicken, Beef, Pork, Cheese, Yogurt) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line series; color/hue; end labels (top chart) |
| Food category (Beef, Almonds, Cheese, Pork, Chicken, Eggs, Lentils, Beans, Green peas) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis as bar categories; text labels (bottom chart) |
| Gallons of water per pound | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis (bottom bar chart) |
| Highlighted category status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (orange for Chicken, yellow for Cheese, muted gray for others in top; corresponding highlights in bottom) |

It's striking to see the immense amounts of water required to produce staples like beef and almonds compared to more water-efficient options like pork and chicken. This insight prompts questions about the sustainability of our food choices and the potential environmental consequences. With this knowledge, we can work towards reducing our collective water usage and mitigating the impact on our environment.
